470.title: Equal in deeds
470.hook: the four castes are equal before their own deeds
470.howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities ordain people of any background, and seniority among monks and nuns is counted from the day of ordination, not from birth or family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first gray hair, the barber's tweezers and a king who called it a messenger. Did you treat one sign of time as a messenger? Day four hundred seventy, a new week.

This conversation happens after the Buddha has died. His disciple Mahākaccāna, a monk remembered for opening up short teachings at length, is staying in a grove near the city of Madhurā. The king of Madhurā comes to see him with a question that's been circulating. Some brahmins of that time held that their class was the highest: born from Brahmā's own mouth, fair where others were dark, pure where others weren't. What does the monk say to that? Mahākaccāna doesn't answer with a slogan. He asks the king to look at how the world actually works.
screen: `AFTER THE BUDDHA'S DEATH.` → `MAHĀKACCĀNA AT MADHURĀ.` → `IS ONE CLASS THE HIGHEST?`

segments.voice: Society at the time was described in four classes: nobles and warriors, brahmins or priests, merchants, and laborers. Mahākaccāna takes them one test at a time. First, money. Suppose a noble becomes rich. Will people of every class rise before him, run his errands, speak pleasantly to win his favor? Yes, says the king. And if a laborer becomes rich? The same. Then in this, he says, the four classes are equal. Second, conduct. If a person of any class kills, steals, lies, what happens after death, as you understand it? Rebirth in a bad state, whatever their class. And if they live well? A good rebirth, whatever their class. Equal again. Third, the law. If a thief is caught breaking into a house, does your court ask his class before punishing him? No. The same punishment for all. Fourth, the spiritual life. If someone of any class shaves their head and goes forth and lives well, do you honor them as a monk? Yes, the king says, whatever their birth. Test after test, the same answer. Equal in deeds. Mahākaccāna isn't saying everyone is identical, or that background doesn't shape a life. He's saying that when it counts, in what people do and what follows from it, birth doesn't settle anything. At the end, the king asks where the Buddha is now. He has passed away, Mahākaccāna says. And the king goes for refuge to the Buddha who has passed, the teaching, and the community. The teacher was gone; the teaching was still answering questions.
screen: `MONEY: EVERYONE SERVES THE RICH.` · `CONDUCT: THE SAME RESULTS.` · `THE LAW: THE SAME PUNISHMENT.` · `GOING FORTH: THE SAME HONOR.` · then, large: `NOT BY BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat everyone as equal today. Sit and settle. Picture the people you'll meet: someone serving you coffee, someone senior at work, someone sleeping in a doorway, someone in a nice car. Notice any small shift in how you'd greet each one. Don't scold yourself. Just see it. Then picture greeting each with the same eyes and the same voice. Let that be your intention as you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Equal in deeds. Mahākaccāna's four tests, money, conduct, the law and going forth, and the same answer each time: birth doesn't settle it. Today's word.
Your line: not by birth. Today, greet one person you'd usually overlook exactly the way you'd greet someone important. Day four hundred seventy.

it's after his death; the king takes refuge in the Buddha who has passed.
Mahākaccāna answers by asking the king questions
four tests, each answered by the king himself.
the sutta claims everyone's life is identical, whatever their background
it says birth doesn't settle what matters: deeds and their results.

fork.setup: you're the king's judge. a thief is caught breaking into a house. what do you ask first?
options: what class he was born into
fork.reveal: the king admits the law punishes a thief of any class the same way. Mahākaccāna: then in this, the four are equal.

original.note: Pali vaṇṇa (Sanskrit varṇa): color, class. the four vaṇṇas are the four social classes the sutta discusses.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha simply abolished caste.
what it means: in this sutta a disciple shows, test by test, that birth doesn't decide wealth's privileges, moral results, justice or spiritual honor.
what a scholar hears: MN 84, the Madhurā Sutta, is set after the Buddha's parinibbāna, and its arguments recur in MN 93 and MN 96.

471.title: Angulimala, read whole
471.hook: the story from year one, now read in full
471.howItsDone: Angulimāla's verse of truth for a safe birth, the Aṅgulimāla Paritta, is still chanted by monks in Theravada countries for expectant mothers, and his story is told as proof that anyone can change.

segments.voice: Yesterday: equal in deeds, Mahākaccāna's four tests. Your line was not by birth. Who did you greet the way you'd greet someone important? Day four hundred seventy-one.

In year one, back around day seventy, we told this story in pieces: the road, the chase, I have stopped, the woman in labor, the stones. Now we read the eighty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings whole, in order, and some quieter scenes come into view. One of them begins with a king. Pasenadi of Kosala rides out of his capital with five hundred horsemen. His people have been gathering outside the palace, crying out about a killer in the forest. The king is going to hunt Angulimāla down. On the way, he stops to pay respects to the Buddha.
screen: `TOLD IN PIECES, NOW READ WHOLE.` → `FIVE HUNDRED HORSEMEN.` → `A KING ON A HUNT.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks him: what's wrong, great king? Is a neighboring kingdom attacking you? No, says Pasenadi. It's a bandit, Angulimāla. I'm going to put him down. And the Buddha asks him an unexpected question. Suppose you saw Angulimāla with his head shaved, in robes, gone forth, gentle, eating one meal a day, keeping the precepts. What would you do? The king says: I'd bow to him. I'd offer him robes and food and shelter, and protect him. But how could someone like that ever become someone like this? Then the Buddha stretches out his arm and points. There is Angulimāla. The king is terrified, his hair standing on end. The Buddha says: don't be afraid. You have nothing to fear from him. The king walks over, asks his family name, and offers him robes. Angulimāla says he already has his three. Then the king turns back to the Buddha and says it plainly: the one we couldn't tame with punishment or weapons, you've tamed without either. And he rides home. The sutta goes on: the woman in labor, the stones on the alms round, and then Angulimāla alone, freed, speaking verses. One of them is also in the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's words: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." In another verse he says his name had been Harmless, and now, at last, he lives up to it. Read whole, the story isn't only about one man stopping. A king stops too.
screen: `IS A KINGDOM ATTACKING YOU?` · `WHAT IF HE WERE A MONK?` · `THERE IS ANGULIMĀLA.` · `TAMED WITHOUT PUNISHMENT OR WEAPONS.` · then, large: `I HAVE STOPPED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it aloud. If you have the Dhammapada or the sutta nearby, open it and read a few lines out loud, slowly. If not, say Müller's moon verse aloud, once, at the pace of a walk: he who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds. Then sit quietly. Let the picture of the moon coming out from behind a cloud stay with you. The bell holds the time.
Angulimāla. The killer who stopped, read whole: the Buddha on the road, the king with his army, and a man who finally lived up to his name, Harmless. Today's word.
Your line: I have stopped. Today, notice one chase you're on, and stop, even for a minute, the way the king turned his horses home. Day four hundred seventy-one.

original.note: Pali ṭhito ahaṃ: 'I have stopped', the Buddha's answer on the road.

trapdoor: what you thought: Angulimāla's story is about a killer who changed.
what it means: read whole, it's also about a king who came to kill and went home, and a man who grew into his old name, Harmless.
what a scholar hears: MN 86, the Aṅgulimāla Sutta; his verses also appear in the Theragāthā, and the Dhammapada shares the moon verse.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

472.title: Born from the dear
472.hook: a father mad with grief; sorrow comes from what is dear; the king and queen argue it through
472.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on this sutta when helping people with grief, and many Buddhists reflect on the impermanence of loved ones as part of daily practice, alongside loving-kindness toward them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angulimāla, read whole, and a king who rode out to kill and went home. Your line was I have stopped. Which chase did you stop? Day four hundred seventy-two.

This one is about grief, so go gently. A man's only son has died, a small boy. Since then he can't work. He can't eat. He goes to the cremation ground every day and cries out: my only child, where are you? Eventually he comes to the Buddha, who sees at once that something is wrong. Your senses aren't steady, householder. How could they be, he says. My only son is dead. And what the Buddha says next, the man refuses to accept.
screen: `GO GENTLY.` → `MY ONLY CHILD, WHERE ARE YOU?` → `HE REFUSES TO ACCEPT IT.`

segments.voice: So it is, householder, the Buddha says. Sorrow, grief, pain and despair are born from those who are dear. The Pali word is piya, dear, beloved. The father shakes his head. How could that be? Happiness and joy are born from those who are dear. And he walks out, unconvinced. He goes to some men playing dice nearby and tells them the story. They agree with him: happiness comes from the dear, obviously. The talk travels until it reaches the palace. King Pasenadi hears it and tells Queen Mallikā, and she says: if the Buddha said it, it's so. The king snaps at her. You agree with everything he says, like a pupil with a teacher. So Mallikā sends a messenger to ask the Buddha directly, and he gives more examples, each as raw as the first: a woman whose mother died, who went out of her mind with grief; a man who lost his wife. Then Mallikā does something wise. She doesn't argue in general. She asks the king about his own life. Is our daughter, Princess Vajirī, dear to you? Yes. If anything happened to her, would sorrow arise? Yes, terrible sorrow. And the people of your kingdoms? Am I dear to you? Yes, yes. Then by that, she says, you can see what the Buddha meant. The king rises, turns toward where the Buddha is staying, and pays homage. The sutta never tells anyone to stop loving. It names what comes with love: the grief that waits inside it, born from the same person who is dear.
screen: `PIYA: THE DEAR, THE BELOVED.` · `HAPPINESS, SAYS THE FATHER.` · `MALLIKĀ ASKS ABOUT THEIR DAUGHTER.` · `IT NEVER SAYS STOP LOVING.` · then, large: `THE DEAR BRING GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one love, grief included. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone very dear to you, alive or gone. Let the warmth of them come first. Then, gently, let in the other side: how it hurts, or would hurt, to lose them. Don't push either feeling away. Let the love and the ache sit side by side, like two hands holding one cup. Breathe with both. If it's too much, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Born from the dear. Sorrow and grief are born from those we love. A grieving father, a queen's question, and a king who finally saw it. Today's word.
Your line: the dear bring grief. Today, tell someone dear to you that they are, knowing what that costs. Day four hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 472 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY THE OLD KING BOWS.`

fork.reveal: she asks about Princess Vajirī, about the kingdom, about herself. his own answers show him what the Buddha meant.

original.note: Pali piya (Sanskrit priya): dear, beloved. the sutta is the Piyajātika: 'born from the dear'.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving people brings happiness.
what it means: in this sutta, sorrow and grief are born from those who are dear; it never says stop loving.
what a scholar hears: MN 87, the Piyajātika Sutta; the argument is won not by the Buddha in person but by Queen Mallikā, a lay woman, reasoning from the king's own life.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 212–216 (related verses on what is dear)

473.title: Why the old king bows
473.hook: King Pasenadi kisses the Buddha's feet and tells why he loves the community
473.howItsDone: Buddhists bow to the Buddha, the teaching and the community, often three times, at shrines, temples and before teachers, and many describe the bow as an expression of gratitude for what they have seen the practice do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: born from the dear, and Queen Mallikā's question to the king. Your line was the dear bring grief. Did you tell someone dear to you that they are? Day four hundred seventy-three.

King Pasenadi again, but much older now. He's out driving through a park, and the trees are quiet and beautiful, the kind of quiet that makes him think of the Buddha. He asks where the Buddha is staying. It's a fair way off, in a Sakyan town. He goes anyway. At the monastery, he takes off the five signs of a king, the sword, the sunshade, the crown and the rest, and hands them to his general. Then he walks alone to a closed door, coughs, and knocks.
screen: `A QUIET PARK.` → `THE FIVE SIGNS OF A KING, HANDED OVER.` → `A CLOSED DOOR. A KNOCK.`

segments.voice: The Buddha opens the door. And the king of Kosala goes down on the floor, puts his head at the Buddha's feet, kisses them, strokes them, and says his own name: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala. The Buddha asks, why such honor? And the king tells him, reason after reason. I see your monks, he says, living together in harmony, like milk and water, looking at one another with kind eyes. I don't always see that, he says, even among brothers and sisters. I sit in judgment in my own court, and people interrupt me. When you teach hundreds of people, there isn't a sound. Once someone coughed, and the person beside him nudged him: quiet, the Teacher is speaking. Clever people come to trap you with questions, and leave as your followers. My own two chamberlains, men I feed and pay, lie with their heads toward you at night, and their feet toward me. Then the most personal one. The Buddha is a noble, and so am I. He's of Kosala, and so am I. He's eighty, and so am I. That's why I bow. After the king leaves, the Buddha calls these the king's monuments to the Dhamma, and tells the monks to learn them. It's a striking text. A king listing, not miracles or doctrines, but behavior: how monks look at each other, how a room stays quiet, where servants point their heads. The commentaries add a sadder frame. While the king was inside, his general rode off with the royal insignia, and Pasenadi never sat on his throne again. Which makes his last reasons, both of us are eighty, all the more tender.
screen: `I AM PASENADI, KING OF KOSALA.` · `LIKE MILK AND WATER.` · `A ROOM WITHOUT A SOUND.` · `HE'S EIGHTY, AND SO AM I.` · then, large: `WHY I BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say why you value your practice. Sit and settle. Ask yourself, like the king: what have I actually seen, in my own life, that makes this path worth walking? Not a doctrine. Something you've noticed. A calmer morning. A kinder reply. A person whose way of living moved you. Name two or three, quietly, the way Pasenadi counted his. Then rest with them. The bell holds the time.
Why the old king bows. Pasenadi, at eighty, kisses the Buddha's feet and gives his reasons: harmony, quiet, and things he'd seen with his own eyes. Today's word.
screen: `WHY THE OLD KING BOWS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: why I bow. Today, write down or say aloud one real reason your practice matters to you, something you've seen, not just heard. Day four hundred seventy-three.

original.note: Pali dhammacetiya: a monument to the Dhamma. the Buddha's name for the king's reasons.

trapdoor: what you thought: the king bows because the Buddha is holy.
what it means: the king bows for reasons he has seen with his own eyes: harmony, quiet, and two old men walking the same road.
what a scholar hears: MN 89, the Dhammacetiya Sutta; the commentary sets it on the day General Dīgha Kārāyana took the royal insignia and helped put Pasenadi's son Viḍūḍabha on the throne.

474.title: Watching him walk
474.hook: the old brahmin's pupil follows the Buddha for months, watching how he walks and eats
474.howItsDone: Monastic training in Buddhist traditions gives careful attention to deportment, how to walk, sit, eat and wear robes, and lay Buddhists often say they learned most from watching how a respected teacher lives day to day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: why the old king bows, and Pasenadi's reasons, all things he'd seen. Your line was why I bow. What real reason did you name? Day four hundred seventy-four.

How do you really get to know someone? Not their profile, not their speeches. You watch them on an ordinary day. How they treat a waiter. How they eat when they think nobody's looking. In the city of Mithilā lives a famous brahmin named Brahmāyu, a master of the old Vedic learning, and the sutta says he's a hundred and twenty years old. He hears the Buddha is nearby, and he does something careful. He sends his best student, a young man named Uttara, to watch. Not to debate. To watch.
screen: `WATCH THEM ON AN ORDINARY DAY.` → `BRAHMĀYU, A HUNDRED AND TWENTY.` → `NOT TO DEBATE. TO WATCH.`

segments.voice: Uttara follows the Buddha for seven months, the sutta says, like a shadow that never leaves. Then he goes home and reports, down to the smallest movement. When he walks, he steps off with the right foot. His stride is neither too long nor too short. He walks neither too fast nor too slow. His knees and ankles don't knock together. When he looks back, he turns his whole body, the way an elephant does, not just a glance over the shoulder. When he sits down in a house, he doesn't drop into the seat or fidget once he's there. When he eats, he takes rice and curry in proportion. He turns each mouthful over two or three times before swallowing. He tastes the food, the report says, but without greed for the taste. After eating he sits in silence for a while, then gives a blessing for the meal, and he doesn't find fault with the food. When he teaches, his voice is clear and carries exactly as far as the gathering, and no farther. And so it goes: robes, bowl, washing, sleeping. Notice what convinces Uttara. Not an argument. Not a wonder. A man who is the same in the kitchen as on the teaching seat. Brahmāyu hears the report, bows in the Buddha's direction, and later goes to meet him. The sutta says he understood the teaching that day and died not long after. A hundred and twenty years old, and what first reached him was a description of someone eating rice.
screen: `SEVEN MONTHS, LIKE A SHADOW.` · `RIGHT FOOT FIRST, NEITHER FAST NOR SLOW.` · `TASTE WITHOUT GREED.` · `THE SAME IN THE KITCHEN AS ON THE SEAT.` · then, large: `WATCH HOW THEY WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch someone good for a day. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone whose goodness you trust, not from what they say, but from how they are. Picture them doing something ordinary: walking into a room, eating, answering a phone. What do you notice? Then, for the rest of the sit, turn the same quiet attention on yourself: how you're sitting, how you're breathing, right now. The bell holds the time.
Watching him walk. Uttara followed the Buddha for seven months and reported how he walked, sat and ate. What convinced him was the ordinary. Today's word.
Your line: watch how they walk. Today, notice one good person in an ordinary moment, and eat one meal the way Uttara saw it done: tasting, without greed. Day four hundred seventy-four.

send your best student to watch him live
fork.reveal: Brahmāyu sends Uttara to watch. seven months of ordinary days tell him more than any debate.

original.note: Pali iriyāpatha: deportment, the postures of walking, standing, sitting and lying down.

trapdoor: what you thought: watching him walk means admiring the Buddha.
what it means: you know someone by their ordinary conduct, the same in the kitchen as on the teaching seat.

what a scholar hears: MN 91, the Brahmāyu Sutta, combines a check of the thirty-two marks of a great man with this detailed account of deportment; Brahmāyu is said to have reached non-return before he died.

475.title: Any wood makes fire
475.hook: a young brahmin argues caste; fire from any wood burns the same
475.howItsDone: Buddhist communities ordain people of every background, and teachers in South Asia, including the movement led by B. R. Ambedkar, have drawn on suttas like this one in rejecting discrimination by birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: watching him walk, and seven months of Uttara's careful attention. Your line was watch how they walk. Whose ordinary goodness did you notice? Day four hundred seventy-five.

Five hundred brahmins are staying in Sāvatthī, and they're worried. This Gotama is teaching that all four classes can be purified. Someone has to go and argue with him. They choose Assalāyana, sixteen years old, brilliant, already a master of the old texts. He doesn't want to go. The Buddha speaks the Dhamma, he says, and someone who does is hard to argue with. They insist: don't be beaten without a fight. So a sixteen-year-old walks in to debate the Buddha, carrying his elders' claim on his shoulders.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED WORRIED BRAHMINS.` → `ASSALĀYANA, SIXTEEN.` → `DON'T BE BEATEN WITHOUT A FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Assalāyana states the claim as the brahmins of that time held it: brahmins are the highest class, born of Brahmā, from his mouth. The Buddha's first answer is almost blunt. But brahmin women are seen menstruating, pregnant, giving birth and nursing. Brahmins are born from wombs like everyone else. Then he widens the view. In the lands to the northwest, among the Greeks and Kambojans, there are only two classes, masters and servants, and people move from one to the other. So the four-class order isn't a law of nature. Then the gentler tests. Can only a brahmin develop a mind of loving-kindness? No, all four classes can. Can only a brahmin take a back scrubber and bath powder to the river and get clean? No, anyone can. And then the fire. Suppose, the Buddha says, a king gathers a hundred men of different births. He tells those of high birth to make fire with fine woods, sal, pine, lotus, sandalwood. He tells those of low birth to make fire with scraps from a dog's trough, a pig's trough, a washerman's tub, castor-oil wood. Would one fire have flame and color and light, and the other not? Would one cook food and the other not? No, Assalāyana admits. Fire is fire. Whatever the wood, it burns the same and gives the same heat. By the end the young man sits silent, head bowed, and goes for refuge. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "I do not call a man a Brâhmana because of his origin or of his mother." In the Buddhist texts, the word is kept, and given to conduct.
screen: `BORN FROM WOMBS, LIKE EVERYONE.` · `ONLY TWO CLASSES IN THE NORTHWEST.` · `ANYONE CAN BATHE IN THE RIVER.` · `SANDALWOOD OR A PIG'S TROUGH.` · then, large: `ANY WOOD MAKES FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a match. If you have a match or a lighter nearby and it's safe, strike it and watch the flame for a breath or two, then put it out. If not, picture a small flame. Notice: you can't tell what box it came from. Then bring to mind someone you tend to rank below or above you, and picture the same flame in them. Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
Any wood makes fire. Sandalwood or a pig's trough, fire gives the same light and heat. The Buddha's answer to a sixteen-year-old about birth and worth. Today's word.
Your line: any wood makes fire. Today, when you catch yourself judging someone by where they come from, picture the flame. Day four hundred seventy-five.

in the fire test, fire from fine wood burns brighter

fork.setup: a king has a hundred men of different births make fires: some from sandalwood, some from a pig's trough. which fire cooks the food?
options: only the fire of the high-born
fork.reveal: Assalāyana himself admits it: whatever the wood, fire burns the same and serves the same purpose.

original.note: Pali aggi (Sanskrit agni): fire. the image at the heart of the sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: any wood makes fire is a camping tip.
what it means: fire from fine wood or scraps gives the same light and heat; worth doesn't come from birth.
what a scholar hears: MN 93, the Assalāyana Sutta; its mention of the Yona (Greeks) and Kamboja in the northwest is often discussed by historians dating the text.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

476.title: Preserving truth
476.hook: say "this is my belief", not "only this is true"
476.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite this sutta, with the Kālāma Sutta, when encouraging students to hold teachings honestly, saying what they believe and why, and to verify through practice rather than insist on being right.

segments.voice: Yesterday: any wood makes fire, sandalwood or a pig's trough, the same light and heat. When did you picture the flame? Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.

Another sixteen-year-old brahmin, another conversation, another tone entirely. His name is Kāpaṭhika, and he's sitting in a crowd around the Buddha with his elders, including the wealthy brahmin Caṅkī. He keeps interrupting. The Buddha asks him to wait until the elders have finished. Caṅkī speaks up for him: he's learned, he can hold his own in a discussion. So the Buddha turns to him, and Kāpaṭhika asks a real question. Our ancient hymns, he says, have been handed down for generations, and about them we brahmins conclude: only this is true, anything else is wrong. What do you say to that?
screen: `KĀPAṬHIKA, SIXTEEN.` → `CAṄKĪ SPEAKS UP FOR HIM.` → `ONLY THIS IS TRUE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks him: is there a single brahmin, now or in the past seven generations of teachers, who says, I know this, I see this: only this is true? No, Kāpaṭhika admits. Then, he says, it's like a line of blind people, each holding the one in front. The first doesn't see, the middle doesn't see, the last doesn't see. Then he names five ways people come to hold things: faith, liking, tradition, careful reasoning, and a view that seems right after reflection. Each of these, he says, can turn out two ways. Something deeply believed can be empty and false. Something not believed at all can be true. So how does a person preserve the truth? Here's the heart of it. If a person has faith, they preserve the truth when they say: this is my faith. And they don't go further, to the conclusion: only this is true, everything else is wrong. The same with liking, tradition, reasoning: this is what I've received, this is how I reason. Said that way, the truth is kept safe. Notice how modest that is. The Buddha doesn't tell Kāpaṭhika to drop his hymns. He tells him how to hold them honestly. The sutta then goes on to discovering truth, and finally arriving at it, through long practice. But the first step is simply this way of speaking: say what you believe, and how you came to it. That leaves room for the person across the table to do the same.
screen: `A LINE OF BLIND PEOPLE.` · `FIVE WAYS OF HOLDING, EACH CAN GO TWO WAYS.` · `THIS IS MY FAITH.` · `NOT: ONLY THIS IS TRUE.` · then, large: `PRESERVE THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say I believe once. Sit and settle. Bring to mind one thing you hold strongly. Say it silently, the way you usually would, as a plain fact. Then say it again with the Buddha's frame: this is my belief. Or: this is how I reason. Notice how it feels in the body, the difference between the two. Rest in the second way for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Preserving truth. Say this is my faith, this is how I reason, without leaping to only this is true. The Buddha's answer to a sixteen-year-old. Today's word.

Your line: preserve the truth. Say I believe once today, where you'd usually say it's obvious. And that's week sixty-eight: equal in deeds, Angulimāla, born from the dear, the old king, watching him walk, any wood makes fire, and preserving truth. Day four hundred seventy-six.
